name: Camera gear rental marketplace
one_liner: Peer-to-peer lending of camera bodies and lenses between photographers and filmmakers, with damage and theft cover built into every booking.
target_customer: Two-sided: (renters) freelance videographers, indie filmmakers, wedding and event photographers and serious hobbyists who need a specific body or lens for a shoot and want it cheaper and more local than Lensrentals; (owners) the same population on days their gear is idle, plus small rental houses using marketplaces as a demand channel.

existing_products.name: ShareGrid (Backstage / Cast & Crew)
existing_products.pricing: Owner pays a fixed 15% service fee; renter pays a dynamic community fee of typically 10% plus 2.45% + $0.30 card processing. Coverage is mandatory: 'Damage Only' waiver makes the renter liable for 12% of item value on eligible damage (e.g. $180 on a $1,500 item); 'Damage + Theft', Athos short-term and annual insurance are priced at checkout and not published.
existing_products.positioning: Largest US peer-to-peer marketplace for film and photo production gear, local pickup in 100+ US cities plus the UK (absorbed BorrowFox 2019 and KitSplit 2019), with ID verification, an Owner Guarantee and Athos-underwritten insurance.
existing_products.strengths: Category leader since 2013; 150,000+ members; insurance partnership with Athos (specialist entertainment insurer) including voluntary-parting cover; backed since Jan 2022 by Backstage, itself owned by Cast & Crew; deep supply of cinema-grade kit and rental-house listings, not just individuals.
existing_products.weaknesses: Combined take of roughly 25-27% before coverage; owners on forums report rental requests declined and verification friction; coverage pricing opaque until checkout; community fee non-refundable on cancellation; only ~10 employees as of May 2026 per Tracxn, so product velocity is low; effectively US/UK only.
existing_products.traction_signal: Raised ~$1M seed (2016), acquired KitSplit and BorrowFox (2019), acquired by Backstage Jan 2022 (Backstage framed it as entry to a '$10B US production rentals' market). 150,000+ members claimed; Trustpilot only 10 reviews (4 stars); employee count ~10 (Tracxn, May 2026).

existing_products.name: Hygglo (formerly Fat Llama)
existing_products.pricing: After the 24 Nov 2025 brand merge, lender commission 20% + renter fee 10% (Fat Llama previously charged 25% + 25%). Lender Guarantee up to £25,000 per rental in the UK (Fat Llama era figure); protection via Omocom insurance in Nordic markets and a Hygglo Lender Guarantee in UK/US/Canada.
existing_products.positioning: General-purpose 'rent anything' peer-to-peer marketplace (cameras are the largest category) with a lender guarantee; Nordic-founded, operating in Sweden, Norway, Finland, UK, US and Canada.
existing_products.strengths: Scale across categories and countries; Y Combinator alumnus (Fat Llama) that pioneered integrated Hiscox-backed rental insurance; app-store presence; lower fees since the merge; June 2026 rules push all pricing and payment on-platform.
existing_products.weaknesses: Trustpilot (1,500+ reviews for fatllama.com) is full of complaints: lenders say damage claims are 'dodged', support has no phone line, 25% fees each side with 'very little guarantee' (pre-merge); renters rejected after intrusive KYC (passport, bank statements, employment contract, 20-question call); a £140 late fee on a £175 rental; being held liable for a parcel lost in the post. Not camera-specialist, so no cine-grade verification or production-house supply.
existing_products.traction_signal: Fat Llama acquired by Hygglo for £34.5M/$41.5M in Aug 2022; brand retired Nov 2025; HYGGLO LTD active at Companies House; ~1,500 Trustpilot reviews and 288 reviews.io reviews for Fat Llama.

existing_products.name: Wedio
existing_products.pricing: Commission percentages not published in anything I could reach (site blocked from this environment); marketing says rentals include 'global on-demand insurance up to €40,000 per rental'; Trustpilot reviewers cite a £580 excess. Rent-to-own subscriptions from about $63/month for cameras and $69/month for lenses over 3 months.
existing_products.positioning: 'Airbnb of professional film gear' for Europe (Denmark HQ), peer-to-peer rental plus subscription/rent-to-own, insurance included as the headline feature.
existing_products.strengths: 18,000-20,000 active listings worth €36-40M across 1,000+ lenders; ~100,000 monthly creators claimed; €1.25M seed (VF Venture, Founderment, Apr 2023) plus ~€150k Wefunder crowdfunding; strong SEO content footprint in Europe.
existing_products.weaknesses: Trustpilot (~104 reviews) shows repeated claims of £0 payouts on theft, Wedio deducting the owner's rental earnings from reimbursement, the £580 excess leaving smaller items uncovered, and slow claims handling; fee structure not transparent up front.
existing_products.traction_signal: €1.25M seed round April 2023; 18k-20k listings; no 2025-2026 funding or exit news found, which for a 2023 seed company is itself a signal.

existing_products.name: KitSplit
existing_products.pricing: Historically 15-17% owner service fee and 6% renter fee; Damage Waiver from $5; instant insurance (Heffins / OneBeacon) from $150 for rentals over $20k; Owner Guarantee up to $20,000 with a 20% deductible.
existing_products.positioning: New York-founded 'Airbnb for cameras' aimed at professional filmmakers and production companies; acquired by ShareGrid in 2019 but the site still markets to gear owners.
existing_products.strengths: Renters historically paid 30-50% less than rental houses; free automatic owner guarantee; production-company demand side.
existing_products.weaknesses: 20% deductible on the owner guarantee (ShareGrid has none); now a shell brand inside ShareGrid, little independent development since 2019.
existing_products.traction_signal: Raised seed round Feb 2018 (TechCrunch); bought CameraLends 2017; acquired by ShareGrid 2019; most recent public traction data is 2019.

existing_products.name: FriendWithA
existing_products.pricing: Owner pays 10% service fee plus an insurance charge (some owners report ~20% all-in); renter pays 20% service fee plus optional damage protection. Lender Damage Protection up to $10,000 and Lender Liability Guarantee up to $100,000 per rental.
existing_products.positioning: US general-purpose peer-to-peer gear marketplace (sports, outdoor, cameras) with 'camera rentals near me' city landing pages.
existing_products.strengths: Simple protection story with published limits; low listing friction; national SEO coverage per city.
existing_products.weaknesses: Not camera-specialist; coverage capped at $10k which excludes most cine packages; thin supply per city; combined fees ~30-40%.
existing_products.traction_signal: Small: no funding news found; reviews concentrated on affiliate-style review sites rather than Trustpilot.

existing_products.name: Beazy
existing_products.pricing: Fees not published on pages reachable by search; markets itself as free to list with secure payments and verified providers.
existing_products.positioning: European production marketplace combining camera/lighting gear rental with studios and photoshoot locations, targeting content-production teams rather than hobbyists.
existing_products.strengths: Broader wedge (gear + locations + crew logistics) that a pure gear marketplace lacks; Europe-focused.
existing_products.weaknesses: Opaque fees and insurance terms; small brand; overlaps Wedio in the same geography.
existing_products.traction_signal: No funding, user or review-count numbers found.

existing_products.name: Gearbooker
existing_products.pricing: Fees not published in reachable pages; marketing states rentals come with insurance included.
existing_products.positioning: Dutch/Benelux and Nordic city-level peer-to-peer camera, drone and audio rental marketplace ('rent in your own city at low prices').
existing_products.strengths: Dense city landing pages (Amsterdam, Utrecht, Groningen, Copenhagen); insurance included in the rental price.
existing_products.weaknesses: Small, regional; no visible traction numbers; same claim-handling opacity as peers.

existing_products.name: Lensrentals (incl. BorrowLenses)
existing_products.pricing: Example: Sony FX3 body $219-232 for 7 days; LensCap accidental-damage plan ~15% of rental cost, LensCap+ (adds theft/loss) ~25%, renter's maximum liability 10% of replacement value with a plan; shipping extra.
existing_products.positioning: Dominant US owned-inventory rental house shipping nationally, with the Keeper buy-what-you-rent programme and used-gear sales.
existing_products.strengths: 400,000+ copies of 6,000+ products after acquiring BorrowLenses (Mar 2024); reliable, inspected gear; clear protection plans; strong brand and SEO; publishes annual most-rented data.
existing_products.weaknesses: Shipping lead time and cost; typically 15-30% dearer than peer-to-peer; no local same-day pickup outside its Memphis base.
existing_products.traction_signal: Acquired BorrowLenses March 2024; largest inventory in the category; Canon R6 II, Sony FX3 and A7 IV top the 2025 most-rented list.

existing_products.name: Local rental houses, retailer rental desks and informal borrowing
existing_products.pricing: Daily rates roughly 3-5% of item value per day at rental houses (e.g. Adorama Rentals, Camera Rentals NYC, Hunt's, Mike's Camera); informal borrowing via Facebook groups, Discord and film-school networks is free or cash-in-hand with no cover.
existing_products.positioning: The way most working shooters actually solve the problem today: a trusted local house with a certificate-of-insurance requirement, or a friend.
existing_products.strengths: Trust, inspected kit, immediate pickup, relationships; production insurance (COI) already covers house rentals.
existing_products.weaknesses: Requires a COI or large deposits for individuals; limited to big cities; informal borrowing carries the whole theft/damage risk uninsured.
existing_products.traction_signal: Adorama and B&H both run rental arms; the Burbank $100k Arri Alexa theft (2025) and the $34k fake-ID theft from Impulse Cameras show houses bear real fraud losses.

demand_signals: Renting rather than buying is already a mainstream paid behaviour: Lensrentals holds 400,000+ rental copies and analyst reports put global camera-equipment rental at $1.0-3.2B; Backstage justified buying ShareGrid as entry to a '$10B US production rentals' market.

Multiple 'make money renting out your camera gear' guides (ShareGrid, KitSplit, 1kcreatives, howtofilmschool, NCJ Digital, Quora) and side-hustle review sites (sidehusl.com, lushdollar.com) exist, indicating steady owner-side search intent for passive income from idle gear.

Vendor-side listicles ('Top 10 peer-to-peer camera rental marketplaces', PhotoWorkout best-rentals guides, Wedio's own alternatives page) and Quora threads from people asking which apps let them rent gear to others, including someone asking specifically about building 'AirBnb for camera equipment'.

Incumbent complaints are concentrated exactly on the insurance promise: Fat Llama/Hygglo Trustpilot reviews about dodged damage claims and 25% fees; Wedio reviews about £0 payouts, a £580 excess and earnings deducted from reimbursements; KitSplit's 20% deductible criticised in owner comparisons.

Supply-side hardware growth: CIPA reports 9.44M digital camera shipments in 2025 (highest since the pandemic), ~6.3M mirrorless bodies, and consecutive-year growth for the first time in ~20 years, so the idle-gear pool is expanding.

Fraud pressure is a live topic in the segment (Burbank $100k Alexa 35 theft, $34k fake-ID theft from a rental shop, ID-verification vendors such as POY Verify marketing 'fraud prevention for camera rental'), which keeps 'insurance built in' as the buying criterion renters and owners search on.

market.size_estimate: Global camera equipment rental roughly $1.0-3.2B in 2025 depending on the report (MarketGrowthReports $1.03B; Verified/other report mills up to $3.2B), growing 5.8-8.6% CAGR. The peer-to-peer slice is much smaller: my estimate is $100-200M GMV globally (ShareGrid + Hygglo cameras + Wedio + long tail), which at a 25% take rate is $25-50M of platform revenue worldwide. For a solo founder in one country or a handful of cities, the serviceable market is on the order of $5-20M GMV, i.e. $1-5M revenue at best.
market.sizing_method: Top-down from the report-mill figures cross-checked against known player scale: Wedio's 18-20k listings worth ~€40M and 100k monthly creators; ShareGrid's 150k members with ~10 staff; Fat Llama's £34.5M exit price for a multi-category marketplace. Bottom-up sanity check: BLS counts ~50k employed US photographers, other sources 110k+ professionals; if 300k US pros and prosumers rent 3 times a year at ~$150, that is ~$135M of US rental spend addressable by P2P, consistent with the top-down range.
market.growth: Growing single digits. Drivers: creator economy and short-form video demand for cine-style bodies (FX3, R6 II), camera shipments rebounding in 2025-2026, and rising gear prices pushing rent-over-buy. Headwinds: rental houses consolidating (Lensrentals + BorrowLenses) and subscription/rent-to-own models (Grover, Wedio subscription) absorbing part of the demand.

monetisation.payer: Both sides of each transaction: the renter (service fee plus mandatory coverage/damage waiver) and the owner (commission). Insurance/waiver margin is the second revenue line.
monetisation.model: Marketplace take rate on GMV plus a per-booking coverage fee; possible add-ons are verification fees, promoted listings, and annual owner cover.
monetisation.price_point: Defensible envelope from comparables is 15-20% owner commission plus 5-10% renter fee, with a damage-waiver charge of roughly 10-15% of the rental price and renter liability capped at 10-12% of item value. A newcomer would need to undercut the ~25-30% combined take of ShareGrid/Hygglo to attract supply, leaving perhaps 18-22% total.
monetisation.comparable_pricing: ShareGrid 15% owner + ~10% renter + card fees, 12% of value renter liability under Damage Only; Hygglo 20% + 10%; KitSplit 15-17% + 6%, waiver from $5; FriendWithA 10% + insurance from owner, 20% from renter; Lensrentals LensCap ~15% and LensCap+ ~25% of rental; Fat Llama pre-merge 25% + 25% was widely called excessive.
monetisation.acquisition_and_serving_costs: Two-sided cold start per city (no listings means no renters, no renters means owners churn); ID/KYC verification cost per user ($1-3 via Stripe Identity or Persona) and manual review for high-value rentals; insurance loss ratio and fraud (voluntary parting is excluded by most policies and must be self-funded or bought as a rider); dispute handling and customer support that incumbents are criticised for skimping on; chargebacks. Average booking value is low (a $1,500 lens rents for ~$50-75/day), so each dispute can cost more than a month of margin from that owner.

build.mvp_scope: Listings with photos, replacement value and availability calendar; search by city and mount/brand; booking request and owner approval; Stripe Connect payments with pre-authorised security hold; Stripe Identity or Persona KYC for both sides; pickup/return condition photos with timestamps; a written damage-waiver programme (renter liability capped at X% of value) backed by a reserve fund, plus a partner insurance quote flow for high-value items; review system; admin dispute console. Defer: shipping, app, instant book, subscriptions.
build.effort_estimate: Roughly 4-6 months of evenings and weekends (about 400-600 hours) for the software using Nuxt/Vue plus Stripe Connect, Stripe Identity and a hosted search index. The insurance piece is not a software task: expect 2-4 months of parallel effort to get a broker (e.g. Athos, Front Row, Hiscox via a wholesaler, or an embedded provider such as Omocom, Wakim or SureAPX) to quote a contingent/inland-marine programme for a zero-history marketplace, and it may simply be refused until volume exists.

dependencies.name: Insurance partner willing to underwrite P2P short-term gear cover incl. theft/voluntary parting for a new platform (Athos, Front Row, Hiscox, Omocom, Wakim, SureAPX)
Insurance distribution licensing if selling regulated cover rather than a contractual damage waiver (FCA in UK, state producer licences in US)
Maps/geocoding for local search (Google Maps or Mapbox)
Marketplace liquidity: owners must list before renters see value; no third-party API can supply this

usage_frequency: Occasional: most renters need specific gear a few times a year for a shoot; owners list continuously but transact only when a local renter appears. Professional videographers in dense cities may rent monthly, but the agent's bottom-up sizing assumed roughly three rentals a year per active user.
distribution_channels: Local filmmaker and photographer communities in one launch city: r/videography, r/cinematography, r/photography, city-specific Facebook gear groups and Discords, film-school and university media departments (ShareGrid already runs a student programme, so contested but reachable).

Owner recruitment by hand: message people posting gear for sale on MPB/eBay/Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist, and wedding/event photographers with visible kit lists; this is the incumbent playbook (BorrowFox, KitSplit) and is labour-intensive but uncontested per city.
SEO on long-tail 'rent [lens/body] in [city]' terms: ShareGrid, Wedio, Gearbooker and FriendWithA all already run programmatic city pages, so this is contested and slow for a new domain.
Partnering with small rental houses and camera shops as anchor supply (they list on ShareGrid today), which gives a launch city instant inventory and a trusted brand next to the listings.
Content and YouTube collaborations with gear reviewers ('rent before you buy'), and rent-before-you-buy affiliate arrangements with used-gear sellers (MPB, KEH) who lack a rental arm.
differentiation_angles: Transparent claims: publish the waiver terms, excess, payout timelines and an annual claims report; every incumbent is being hammered on Trustpilot for opaque or denied claims, and a small platform can credibly promise a founder-handled 48-hour claim decision. This is positioning and process, not a moat, but it is what owners say they want.

Single-city depth before breadth: incumbents are spread across 100+ cities with thin supply in each; a founder who gets one mid-sized city (not LA/NYC/London) to 300+ verified listings would have better local liquidity than ShareGrid there. Liquidity compounds within a city but does not transfer to the next one.

Owner-first economics: 10-12% owner commission with a small renter fee and coverage priced as a percentage of item value, undercutting the 25-30% combined take at ShareGrid/Hygglo; copyable by incumbents but they have shown reluctance (Hygglo only moved from 50% to 30% combined in 2025).

Specialist verticals incumbents ignore: a specific mount ecosystem (e.g. RF/E-mount telephoto for wildlife and sports), analogue/medium-format, or drone-with-pilot rentals, where community trust and listing quality matter more than scale.

Rental-house-as-supplier hybrid: onboard small houses as verified 'pro' suppliers alongside individuals, giving reliability where P2P is weakest, similar to what ShareGrid already does, so only a wedge, not defensible.
why_now: Camera shipments grew for consecutive years in 2025 for the first time in about 20 years (CIPA), expanding the idle-gear pool, and creator-economy demand for cine-style bodies is rising. There is no technology or regulatory shift that makes a new P2P platform newly possible; the incumbents have run the same model since 2013.
kill_risks: No insurer will bind cover: ask Athos, Front Row and two Lloyd's-market brokers for a contingent inland-marine/rental-gear programme for a zero-history P2P platform; if the answer is 'not until $1M+ annual premium' or exclusions for voluntary parting, the 'insurance built in' promise cannot be delivered and the idea collapses into a self-funded waiver with the founder's savings as the reserve.

Regulatory exposure of the coverage product: check whether a per-booking 'damage waiver' sold by the platform counts as insurance distribution in the launch jurisdiction (FCA in the UK; state insurance departments in the US); several sharing-economy platforms have had to restructure or partner to comply.

Cold-start failure in the launch city: run a 60-day test where 100 owners are hand-recruited in one city and measure whether 30+ real bookings happen without paid acquisition; ShareGrid's 10-person team and Wedio's stall after a 2023 seed suggest liquidity is expensive to buy.

Fraud loss on a single booking wipes out months of margin: one fake-ID renter walking away with a $6,000 FX3 kit (as happened for $34k and $100k at rental shops in 2025) exceeds the total take from ~150 average bookings; check whether ID vendors will guarantee synthetic-ID detection and at what cost.

Incumbent response: ShareGrid (Cast & Crew-backed) and Hygglo can match a lower take rate in a launch city with a promotion; verify whether ShareGrid already has 100+ listings in the intended launch city by searching its city pages before committing.

Owner willingness to lend high-value kit to strangers is thinner than the guides imply: ShareGrid and Wedio reviews include owners who quit after one bad claim, so churn of the supply side after a first incident should be tested early.
recent_moves: Hygglo retired the Fat Llama brand (24 Nov 2025), moved all Fat Llama users to hygglo.com, and cut combined fees from 25%+25% to 20%+10%; a further June 2026 policy change requires all pricing and payment to stay on-platform and repositions its protection as 'Hygglo Care'.

Lensrentals acquired BorrowLenses (March 2024) consolidating US owned-inventory rentals to 400,000+ copies and published a 2025 most-rented list dominated by Sony FX3, A7 IV and Canon R6 II — the exact bodies P2P owners list.

Wedio expanded into subscription and rent-to-own (cameras from ~$63/month, lenses ~$69/month) rather than deepening pure peer-to-peer, suggesting P2P alone was not producing enough revenue after its April 2023 €1.25M seed.
ShareGrid shows no public product announcements in 2025-2026 and roughly 10 employees (Tracxn, May 2026) under Backstage/Cast & Crew, i.e. maintained rather than aggressively developed.
Camera shipments grew for consecutive years for the first time in ~20 years (CIPA, reported Feb 2026), expanding the base of owners with rentable gear.

problem_severity.rationale: Renting is occasional for most shooters and Lensrentals plus seven P2P incumbents already serve the need; the live pain is unreliable claims handling, a workaround-level complaint. Rental volume figures come from acquisition press coverage, complaints from Trustpilot summaries.

market_size.rationale: Global camera rental is $1-3B by report mills that disagree threefold; the P2P slice is the agent's own $100-200M GMV estimate, implying $25-50M platform revenue worldwide and a $1-5M ceiling for a one-country player.

competition.rationale: Seven direct players own the 'P2P with insurance built in' positioning, but their weaknesses are loud and repeated: dodged claims and intrusive KYC at Hygglo (1,500+ Trustpilot reviews), £0 payouts and a £580 excess at Wedio, a 20% deductible at KitSplit. Crowded but fragmented with cited weaknesses is the anchor-3 wording.

differentiation.rationale: Transparent claims, lower commission and single-city depth are positioning and process differences ShareGrid or Hygglo could copy with effort; city liquidity does not compound across cities.

monetisation.rationale: Both sides pay and comparables are documented (ShareGrid 15% + ~10%, Hygglo 20% + 10%, KitSplit 15-17% + 6%), but insurance loss ratios, fraud and small booking values make margins uncertain.

retention.rationale: Episodic need: a few rentals a year for most users, with owner churn after a first bad claim reported in ShareGrid and Wedio reviews. Frequency is the agent's assumption, not measured.

feasibility.rationale: 4-6 months of solo software work, but the sellable version depends on an insurer covering a zero-history platform including theft (Athos documents the voluntary-parting exclusion) and possibly on insurance-distribution licensing; either can refuse indefinitely.

distribution.rationale: Concentrated, reachable communities (city filmmaker groups, film schools, gear-sale listings) and hand-recruiting owners in one city is feasible, but ShareGrid runs student programmes and city SEO, and both sides must be worked at once.

founder_fit.rationale: No founder profile filled in; scored as an adequate-fit solo full-stack developer with no film, photo or insurance background.

timing_and_risk.rationale: No enabling shift: the model has existed since 2013 and Lumoid, KitSplit and Fat Llama have already been absorbed or shut. Meaningful external risk in insurance underwriting, distribution licensing and fraud exposure with no mitigation.

confidence_rationale: Every WebFetch to competitor sites, support pages, Trustpilot and market-report pages was blocked by the network egress proxy, so all pricing and traction figures come from search-result snippets quoting those pages rather than the pages themselves (ShareGrid and KitSplit fee figures are quoted from their own support articles; Hygglo fees from its Fat Llama migration page; Lensrentals prices from product listings). Wedio, Beazy and Gearbooker fees are effectively hidden. Market sizing rests on low-quality report mills that disagree by 3x, and the peer-to-peer slice is my own estimate. Trustpilot complaint themes are from search summaries, not a read of the review pages.
